{{Short description|Mathematical technique in thermal field theory}}
{{one source|date=September 2011}}

In [[thermal quantum field theory]], the '''Matsubara summation''' (named after [[Takeo Matsubara]]) is a technique used to simplify calculations involving [[Path integral formulation#Euclidean path integrals|Euclidean (imaginary time) path integrals]].<ref name="Altland Simons 2010 p. ">{{cite book | last1=Altland | first1=Alexander | last2=Simons | first2=Ben D. | title=Condensed Matter Field Theory | publisher=Cambridge University Press | date=2010-03-11 | isbn=978-0-521-76975-4 | doi=10.1017/cbo9780511789984 | page=}}</ref>

In thermal quantum field theory, bosonic and fermionic quantum fields <math>\phi(\tau)</math> are respectively periodic or antiperiodic in imaginary time <math>\tau</math>, with periodicity <math>\beta = \hbar / k_{\rm B} T</math>. Matsubara summation refers to the technique of expanding these fields in Fourier series

<math display="block">\phi(\tau) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\beta}}\sum_{n} e^{-i\omega_n \tau}\phi(i\omega_n)
\iff
\phi(i\omega_n) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\beta}} \int_0^\beta d\tau\ e^{i\omega_n \tau}\phi(\tau).</math>

The frequencies <math>\omega_n</math> are called the '''Matsubara frequencies''', taking values from either of the following sets (with <math>n\in\mathbb{Z}</math>):
*bosonic frequencies: <math>\omega_n=\frac{2n\pi}{\beta},</math>
*fermionic frequencies: <math>\omega_n=\frac{(2n+1)\pi}{\beta},</math>
which respectively enforce periodic and antiperiodic boundary conditions on the field <math>\phi(\tau)</math>.  

Once such substitutions have been made, certain diagrams contributing to the action take the form of a so-called Matsubara summation

<math display="block">
S_\eta = \frac{1}{\beta}\sum_{i\omega_n} g(i\omega_n).
</math>

The summation will converge if <math>g(z=i\omega)</math> tends to 0 in <math>z\to\infty</math> limit in a manner faster than <math>z^{-1}</math>. The summation over bosonic frequencies is denoted as <math>S_{\rm B}</math> (with <math>\eta=+1</math>), while that over fermionic frequencies is denoted as <math>S_{\rm F}</math> (with <math>\eta=-1</math>). <math>\eta</math> is the statistical sign.

In addition to thermal quantum field theory, the Matsubara frequency summation method also plays an essential role in the diagrammatic approach to [[solid-state physics]], namely, if one  considers the diagrams at finite temperature.<ref>[[Alexei Alekseyevich Abrikosov|A. Abrikosov]], [[Lev Gor'kov|L. Gor'kov]], [[Igor Dzyaloshinskii|I. Dzyaloshinskii]]: ''Methods of Quantum Field Theory in Statistical Physics.'', New York, Dover Publ., 1975, {{ISBN|0-486-63228-8}}</ref>
<ref>[Piers Coleman]: ''Introduction to Many-Body Physics.'', Cambridge University Press., 2015, {{ISBN|978-0-521-86488-6}}</ref>
<ref name=":0">{{Cite book |last=Mahan |first=Gerald D. |title=Many-particle physics |date=2000 |publisher=Kluwer Academic/Plenum Publishers |isbn=0-306-46338-5 |edition=3rd |location=New York |oclc=43864386}}</ref>

Generally speaking, if at <math>T=0\,\text{K}</math>, a  certain [[Feynman diagram]] is represented by an integral <math display="inline">\int_{T=0}  \mathrm{ d}\omega \ g(\omega )</math>, at finite temperature it is given by the sum <math>S_\eta</math>.

== Summation formalism ==

=== General formalism ===
[[Image:Matsubara frequency 1.svg|thumb|168px|Figure 1.]]
[[Image:Matsubara frequency 2.svg|thumb|168px|Figure 2.]]

The trick to evaluate Matsubara frequency summation is to use a Matsubara weighting function ''h''<sub>''η''</sub>(''z'') that has simple [[Pole (complex analysis)|poles]] located exactly at <math> z=i\omega_n</math>.<ref name=":0" /> The weighting functions in the boson case ''η''&nbsp;=&nbsp;+1 and fermion case ''η''&nbsp;=&nbsp;−1 differ. The choice of weighting function will be discussed later. With the weighting function, the summation can be replaced by a contour integral surrounding the imaginary axis.
<math display="block">S_\eta=\frac{1}{\beta}\sum_{i\omega} g(i\omega)=\frac{1}{2\pi i\beta}\oint g(z) h_\eta(z) \,dz,</math>
As in Fig. 1, the weighting function generates poles (red crosses) on the imaginary axis. The contour integral picks up the [[Residue (complex analysis)|residue]] of these poles, which is equivalent to the summation. This procedure is sometimes called Sommerfeld-Watson transformation.<ref>''[https://www.phys.uconn.edu/~rozman/Courses/P2400_16S/downloads/sommerfeld-watson.pdf Summation of series: Sommerfeld-Watson transformation, Lecture notes]'', M. G. Rozman</ref>

By deformation of the contour lines to enclose the poles of ''g''(''z'') (the green cross in Fig. 2), the summation can be formally accomplished by summing the residue of ''g''(''z'')''h''<sub>''η''</sub>(''z'') over all poles of ''g''(''z''),

<math display="block">S_\eta=-\frac 1 \beta \sum_{z_0\in g(z)\text{ poles}} \operatorname{Res} g(z_0) h_\eta(z_0).</math>

Note that a minus sign is produced, because the contour is deformed to enclose the poles in the clockwise direction, resulting in the negative residue.

=== Choice of Matsubara weighting function ===
To produce simple poles on boson frequencies <math>z=i\omega_n</math>, either of the following two types of Matsubara weighting functions can be chosen
<math display="block">h_{\rm B}^{(1)}(z)=\frac{\beta}{1-e^{-\beta z}}=-\beta n_{\rm B}(-z)=\beta(1+n_{\rm B}(z)),</math>
<math display="block">h_{\rm B}^{(2)}(z)=\frac{-\beta}{1-e^{\beta z}}=\beta n_{\rm B}(z),</math>
depending on which half plane the convergence is to be controlled in. <math>h_{\rm B}^{(1)}(z)</math> controls the convergence in the left half plane (Re&nbsp;''z''&nbsp;<&nbsp;0), while <math>h_{\rm B}^{(2)}(z)</math> controls the convergence in the right half plane (Re&nbsp;''z''&nbsp;>&nbsp;0). Here <math>n_{\rm B}(z)=(e^{\beta z}-1)^{-1}</math> is the [[Bose–Einstein statistics|Bose–Einstein]] distribution function.

The case is similar for fermion frequencies. There are also two types of Matsubara weighting functions that produce simple poles at <math>z=i\omega_m</math>
<math display="block">h_{\rm F}^{(1)}(z)=\frac{\beta}{1+e^{-\beta z}}=\beta n_{\rm F}(-z)=\beta(1-n_{\rm F}(z)),</math>
<math display="block">h_{\rm F}^{(2)}(z)=\frac{-\beta}{1+e^{\beta z}}=-\beta n_{\rm F}(z).</math>
<math>h_{\rm F}^{(1)}(z)</math> controls the convergence in the left half plane (Re&nbsp;''z''&nbsp;<&nbsp;0), while <math>h_{\rm F}^{(2)}(z)</math> controls the convergence in the right half plane (Re&nbsp;''z''&nbsp;>&nbsp;0). Here <math>n_{\rm F} (z)=(e^{\beta z}+1)^{-1}</math> is the [[Fermi–Dirac statistics|Fermi–Dirac]] distribution function.

In the application to [[Green's function]] calculation, ''g''(''z'') always have the structure
<math display="block">g(z)=G(z)e^{-z\tau},</math>
which diverges in the left half plane given 0&nbsp;<&nbsp;''τ''&nbsp;<&nbsp;''β''. So as to control the convergence, the weighting function of the first type is always chosen <math>h_\eta(z)=h_\eta^{(1)}(z)</math>. However, there is no need to control the convergence if the Matsubara summation does not diverge. In that case, any choice of the Matsubara weighting function will lead to identical results.

== Applications in physics ==

=== Zero temperature limit ===
In this limit <math>\beta\rightarrow\infty</math>, the Matsubara frequency summation is equivalent to the integration of imaginary frequency over imaginary axis.
<math display="block">\frac{1}{\beta}\sum_{i\omega}=\int_{-i\infty}^{i\infty}\frac{\mathrm{d}(i\omega)}{2\pi i}.</math>
Some of the integrals do not converge. They should be regularized by introducing the frequency cutoff <math>\Omega</math>, and then subtracting the divergent part (<math>\Omega</math>-dependent) from the integral before taking the limit of <math>\Omega\rightarrow\infty</math>. For example, the free energy is obtained by the integral of logarithm,
<math display="block">\eta \lim_{\Omega\rightarrow\infty}\left[
\int_{-i\Omega}^{i\Omega}\frac{\mathrm{d}(i\omega)}{2\pi i} \left(\ln(-i\omega+\xi)-\frac{\pi\xi}{2\Omega}\right)-\frac{\Omega}{\pi}(\ln\Omega-1)\right]
=\left\{ 
\begin{array}{cc}
 0 & \xi\geq0, \\
 -\eta\xi & \xi<0,
\end{array}
\right.
</math>
meaning that at zero temperature, the free energy simply relates to the [[internal energy]] below the [[chemical potential]]. Also the distribution function is obtained by the following integral
<math display="block">\eta \lim_{\Omega\rightarrow\infty}
\int_{-i\Omega}^{i\Omega}\frac{\mathrm{d}(i\omega)}{2\pi i} \left(\frac{1}{-i\omega+\xi}-\frac{\pi}{2\Omega}\right)
=\left\{ 
\begin{array}{cc}
 0 & \xi\geq0, \\
 -\eta & \xi<0,
\end{array}
\right.
</math>
which shows step function behavior at zero temperature.

=== Green's function related ===

==== Time domain ====
Consider a function ''G''(''τ'') defined on the imaginary time interval (0,''β''). It can be given in terms of [[Fourier series]],

<math display="block">G(\tau)=\frac{1}{\beta}\sum_{i\omega} G(i\omega) e^{-i\omega\tau},</math>

where the frequency only takes discrete values spaced by&nbsp;2{{pi}}/''β''.

The particular choice of frequency depends on the boundary condition of the function ''G''(''τ''). In physics, ''G''(''τ'') stands for the imaginary time representation of Green's function

<math display="block">G(\tau)=-\langle \mathcal{T}_\tau \psi(\tau)\psi^*(0) \rangle. </math>

It satisfies the periodic boundary condition ''G''(''τ''+''β'')=''G''(''τ'') for a boson field. While for a fermion field the boundary condition is anti-periodic ''G''(''τ''&nbsp;+&nbsp;''β'')&nbsp;=&nbsp;−''G''(''τ'').

Given the Green's function ''G''(''iω'') in the [[frequency domain]], its imaginary time representation ''G''(''τ'') can be evaluated by Matsubara frequency summation. Depending on the boson or fermion frequencies that is to be summed over, the resulting ''G''(''τ'') can be different. To distinguish, define
<math display="block">G_\eta(\tau)= \begin{cases}
  G_{\rm B}(\tau), & \text{if } \eta = +1, \\
  G_{\rm F}(\tau), & \text{if } \eta = -1,
\end{cases}
</math>
with
<math display="block">G_{\rm B}(\tau)=\frac{1}{\beta}\sum_{i\omega_n}G(i\omega_n)e^{-i\omega_n\tau},</math>
<math display="block">G_{\rm F}(\tau)=\frac{1}{\beta}\sum_{i\omega_m}G(i\omega_m)e^{-i\omega_m\tau}.</math>

Note that ''τ'' is restricted in the principal interval (0,''β''). The boundary condition can be used to extend ''G''(''τ'') out of the principal interval. Some frequently used results are concluded in the following table.

{| class="wikitable"
|-
!<math>G(i\omega)</math>
!<math>G_\eta(\tau)</math>
|- 
|<math>(i\omega-\xi)^{-1}</math>
|<math>-e^{\xi(\beta-\tau)}n_\eta(\xi)</math>
|-
|<math>(i\omega-\xi)^{-2}</math>
|<math>e^{\xi(\beta-\tau)}n_\eta(\xi)\left(\tau+\eta\beta n_\eta(\xi)\right)</math>
|-
|<math>(i\omega-\xi)^{-3}</math>
|<math>-\frac{1}{2}e^{\xi(\beta-\tau)}n_\eta(\xi) \left(\tau^2+\eta\beta(\beta+2\tau) n_\eta(\xi)+2\beta^2n^2_\eta(\xi)\right)</math>
|-
|<math>(i\omega-\xi_1)^{-1}(i\omega-\xi_2)^{-1}</math>
|<math>-\frac{e^{\xi_1(\beta-\tau)}n_\eta(\xi_1)-e^{\xi_2(\beta-\tau)}n_\eta(\xi_2)}{\xi_1-\xi_2}</math>
|-
|<math>(\omega^2+m^2)^{-1}</math>
|<math>\frac{e^{-m\tau}}{2m}+\frac{\eta}{m}\cosh{m\tau}\;n_\eta(m)</math>
|-
|<math>i\omega(\omega^2+m^2)^{-1}</math>
|<math>\frac{e^{-m\tau}}{2}-\eta\,\sinh{m\tau}\;n_\eta(m)</math>
|-
|}

==== Operator switching effect ====
The small imaginary time plays a critical role here. The order of the operators will change if the small imaginary time changes sign.
<math display="block">\langle \psi\psi^*\rangle=\langle \mathcal{T}_\tau \psi(\tau=0^+) \psi^*(0)\rangle
=-G_\eta(\tau=0^+)=-\frac{1}{\beta}\sum_{i\omega}G(i\omega)e^{-i\omega 0^+}</math>
<math display="block">\langle \psi^*\psi\rangle=\eta\langle \mathcal{T}_\tau \psi(\tau=0^-) \psi^*(0)\rangle
=-\eta G_\eta(\tau=0^-)=-\frac{\eta}{\beta}\sum_{i\omega}G(i\omega)e^{i\omega 0^+}</math>

==== Distribution function ====
The evaluation of distribution function becomes tricky because of the discontinuity of Green's function ''G''(''τ'') at ''τ''&nbsp;=&nbsp;0. To evaluate the summation
<math display="block"> G(0) = \sum_{i\omega}(i\omega-\xi)^{-1},</math>
both choices of the weighting function are acceptable, but the results are different. This can be understood if we push ''G''(''τ'') away from ''τ''&nbsp;=&nbsp;0 a little bit, then to control the convergence, we must take <math>h_\eta^{(1)}(z)</math> as the weighting function for <math>G(\tau=0^+)</math>, and <math>h_\eta^{(2)}(z)</math> for <math>G(\tau=0^-)</math>.

Bosons
<math display="block">G_{\rm B}(\tau=0^-)=\frac{1}{\beta}\sum_{i\omega_n}\frac{e^{i\omega_n 0^+}}{i\omega_n-\xi}=-n_{\rm B}(\xi),</math>
<math display="block">G_{\rm B}(\tau=0^+)=\frac{1}{\beta}\sum_{i\omega_n}\frac{e^{-i\omega_n 0^+}}{i\omega_n-\xi}=-(n_{\rm B}(\xi)+1).</math>
Fermions
<math display="block">G_{\rm F}(\tau=0^-)=\frac{1}{\beta}\sum_{i\omega_m}\frac{e^{i\omega_m 0^+}}{i\omega_m-\xi}=n_{\rm F}(\xi),</math>
<math display="block">G_{\rm F}(\tau=0^+)=\frac{1}{\beta}\sum_{i\omega_m}\frac{e^{-i\omega_m 0^+}}{i\omega_m-\xi}=n_{\rm F}(\xi)-1.</math>

==== Free energy ====
Bosons
<math display="block">\frac{1}{\beta}\sum_{i\omega_n} \ln(\beta(-i\omega_n+\xi))=\frac{1}{\beta}\ln(1-e^{-\beta\xi}),</math>
Fermions
<math display="block">-\frac{1}{\beta}\sum_{i\omega_m} \ln(\beta(-i\omega_m+\xi))=-\frac{1}{\beta}\ln(1+e^{-\beta\xi}).</math>

=== Diagram evaluations ===
Frequently encountered diagrams are evaluated here with the single mode setting. Multiple mode problems can be approached by a spectral function integral.
Here <math>\omega_m</math> is a fermionic Matsubara frequency, while <math>\omega_n</math> is a bosonic Matsubara frequency.

==== Fermion self energy ====
<math display="block">\Sigma(i\omega_m)=-\frac{1}{\beta }\sum _{i \omega_n } \frac{1}{i \omega_m +i \omega_n -\varepsilon }\frac{1}{i \omega_n -\Omega }=\frac{n_{\rm F}(\varepsilon )+n_{\rm B}(\Omega )}{i \omega_m -\varepsilon +\Omega }.</math>

==== Particle-hole bubble ====
<math display="block">\Pi (i \omega_n )=\frac{1}{\beta }\sum _{i \omega_m } \frac{1}{i \omega_m +i \omega_n -\varepsilon }\frac{1}{i \omega_m -\varepsilon '}=-\frac{n_{\rm F}(\varepsilon )-n_{\rm F} \left(\varepsilon '\right)}{i \omega_n -\varepsilon +\varepsilon'}.</math>

==== Particle-particle bubble ====
<math display="block">\Pi (i \omega_n )=-\frac{1}{\beta }\sum _{i \omega_m } \frac{1}{i \omega_m +i \omega_n -\varepsilon }\frac{1}{-i \omega_m -\varepsilon '}=\frac{1-n_{\rm F}\left(\varepsilon '\right) - n_{\rm F}(\varepsilon )}{i \omega_n -\varepsilon -\varepsilon '}.</math>

== Appendix: Properties of distribution functions ==

=== Distribution functions ===
The general notation <math>n_\eta</math> stands for either Bose (''η''&nbsp;=&nbsp;+1) or Fermi (''η''&nbsp;=&nbsp;−1) distribution function
<math display="block">n_\eta(\xi)=\frac{1}{e^{\beta\xi}-\eta}.</math>
If necessary, the specific notations ''n''<sub>B</sub> and ''n''<sub>F</sub> are used to indicate Bose and Fermi distribution functions respectively
<math display="block">n_\eta(\xi)= \begin{cases}
  n_{\rm B}(\xi), & \text{if } \eta = +1, \\
  n_{\rm F}(\xi), & \text{if } \eta = -1.
\end{cases}
</math>

=== Relation to hyperbolic functions ===
The Bose distribution function is related to hyperbolic cotangent function by
<math display="block">n_{\rm B}(\xi)=\frac{1}{2}\left(\operatorname{coth}\frac{\beta\xi}{2}-1\right).</math>
The Fermi distribution function is related to hyperbolic tangent function by
<math display="block">n_{\rm F}(\xi)=\frac{1}{2}\left(1-\operatorname{tanh}\frac{\beta\xi}{2}\right).</math>

=== Parity ===
Both distribution functions do not have definite parity,
<math display="block">n_\eta(-\xi)=-\eta-n_\eta(\xi).</math>
Another formula is in terms of the <math>c_\eta</math> function
<math display="block">n_\eta(-\xi)=n_\eta(\xi)+2\xi c_\eta(0,\xi).</math>
However their derivatives have definite parity.

=== Bose–Fermi transmutation ===
Bose and Fermi distribution functions transmute under a shift of the variable by the fermionic frequency,
<math display="block">n_\eta(i\omega_m+\xi)=-n_{-\eta}(\xi).</math>
However shifting by bosonic frequencies does not make any difference.

=== Derivatives ===

==== First order ====
<math display="block">n_{\rm B}^\prime(\xi)=-\frac{\beta}{4}\mathrm{csch}^2\frac{\beta \xi}{2},</math>
<math display="block">n_{\rm F}^\prime(\xi)=-\frac{\beta}{4}\mathrm{sech}^2\frac{\beta \xi}{2}.</math>
In terms of product:
<math display="block">n_\eta^\prime(\xi)= -\beta n_\eta(\xi)(1+\eta n_\eta(\xi)).</math>
In the zero temperature limit:
<math display="block">n_\eta^\prime(\xi)=\eta\delta(\xi) \text{ as } \beta\rightarrow\infty.</math>

==== Second order ====
<math display="block">n_{\rm B}^{\prime\prime}(\xi)=\frac{\beta^2}{4}\operatorname{csch}^2\frac{\beta \xi}{2}\operatorname{coth}\frac{\beta \xi}{2},</math>
<math display="block">n_{\rm F}^{\prime\prime}(\xi)=\frac{\beta^2}{4}\operatorname{sech}^2\frac{\beta \xi}{2}\operatorname{tanh}\frac{\beta \xi}{2}.</math>

=== Formula of difference ===
<math display="block">n_\eta(a+b)-n_\eta(a-b)=-\frac{\mathrm{sinh}\beta b}{\mathrm{cosh}\beta a-\eta\,\mathrm{cosh}\beta b}.</math>

==== Case ''a'' = 0 ====
<math display="block">n_{\rm B}(b)-n_{\rm B}(-b)=\mathrm{coth}\frac{\beta b}{2},</math>
<math display="block">n_{\rm F}(b)-n_{\rm F}(-b)=-\mathrm{tanh}\frac{\beta b}{2}.</math>

==== Case ''a'' → 0 ====
<math display="block">n_{\rm B}(a+b)-n_{\rm B}(a-b)=\operatorname{coth}\frac{\beta b}{2}+n_{\rm B}^{\prime\prime}(b)a^2+\cdots,</math>
<math display="block">n_{\rm F}(a+b)-n_{\rm F}(a-b)=-\operatorname{tanh}\frac{\beta b}{2}+n_{\rm F}^{\prime\prime}(b)a^2+\cdots.</math>

==== Case ''b'' → 0 ====
<math display="block">n_{\rm B}(a+b)-n_{\rm B}(a-b)=2n_{\rm B}^\prime(a)b+\cdots,</math>
<math display="block">n_{\rm F}(a+b)-n_{\rm F}(a-b)=2n_{\rm F}^\prime(a)b+\cdots.</math>

=== The function ''c''<sub>''η''</sub> ===
Definition:
<math display="block">c_\eta(a,b)\equiv-\frac{n_\eta(a+b)-n_\eta(a-b)}{2b}.</math>
For Bose and Fermi type:
<math display="block">c_{\rm B}(a,b)\equiv c_+(a,b),</math>
<math display="block">c_{\rm F}(a,b)\equiv c_-(a,b).</math>

==== Relation to hyperbolic functions ====
<math display="block">c_\eta(a,b)=\frac{\sinh\beta b}{2b(\cosh\beta a-\eta\cosh\beta b)}.</math>
It is obvious that <math>c_{\rm F}(a,b)</math> is positive definite.

To avoid overflow in the numerical calculation, the tanh and coth functions are used
<math display="block">c_{\rm B}(a,b)=\frac{1}{4b}\left(\operatorname{coth}\frac{\beta(a-b)}{2} - \operatorname{coth}\frac{\beta(a+b)}{2}\right),</math>
<math display="block">c_{\rm F}(a,b)=\frac{1}{4b}\left(\operatorname{tanh}\frac{\beta(a+b)}{2} - \operatorname{tanh}\frac{\beta(a-b)}{2}\right).</math>

==== Case ''a'' = 0 ====
<math display="block">c_{\rm B}(0,b)=-\frac{1}{2b}\operatorname{coth}\frac{\beta b}{2},</math>
<math display="block">c_{\rm F}(0,b)=\frac{1}{2b}\operatorname{tanh}\frac{\beta b}{2}.</math>

==== Case ''b'' = 0 ====
<math display="block">c_{\rm B}(a,0)=\frac{\beta}{4}\operatorname{csch}^2\frac{\beta a}{2},</math>
<math display="block">c_{\rm F}(a,0)=\frac{\beta}{4}\operatorname{sech}^2\frac{\beta a}{2}.</math>

==== Low temperature limit ====

For ''a'' = 0: <math>c_{\rm F}(0,b)=\frac{1}{2|b|}.</math>

For ''b'' = 0: <math>c_{\rm F}(a,0)=\delta(a).</math>

In general,
<math display="block">c_{\rm F}(a,b)=\begin{cases}
  \frac{1}{2|b|}, & \text{if } |a|<|b| \\
  0,  & \text{if } |a|>|b|
\end{cases}</math>
